Diet
di'et
n. (a regular allowance of food; the daily provision assigned to a person)
Greek diaita, a way of living, from which Latin diaeta and French diete. The older sense is not what one eats to lose weight but the settled provision by which one lives.

Biblical Definition

The word occurs once, and it closes the book of Jeremiah — a book that began with a nation under sentence and ends with a captive king at a foreign table. Jehoiachin, carried to Babylon as a youth and imprisoned thirty-seven years, is released by Evil-merodach: “And for his diet, there was a continual diet given him of the king of Babylon, every day a portion until the day of his death, all the days of his life” (Jer 52:34). The parallel account adds that his prison garments were changed and that he ate bread continually before the king. Note the words continual, every day, all the days of his life — Jeremiah piles them up. It is the last note of a book of judgment, and it is a note of preservation: the line of David is not extinct, it is fed at a pagan king's table, and Matthew's genealogy will run straight through this man to Christ. Scripture repeatedly ends its darkest sections with a daily provision rather than a dramatic rescue — the same pattern as manna, as the widow's barrel, and as the petition the Lord taught: give us this day our daily bread.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines diet as food or victuals; a regular course of eating and drinking prescribed; and an allowance of provision.

expand to see more

DI'ET, n. [Gr. diaita, manner of living; L. diaeta.]

1. Food or victuals.

2. Food prescribed by a physician, with respect to quantity and quality.

3. Allowance of provision. For his diet, there was a continual diet given him of the king of Babylon. Jer. 52.

DI'ET, v.t. To feed; to board; to furnish provisions for.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 52:34 — "And for his diet, there was a continual diet given him of the king of Babylon, every day a portion until the day of his death, all the days of his life."

Jeremiah 52:33 — "And changed his prison garments: and he did continually eat bread before him all the days of his life."

2 Kings 25:30 — "And his allowance was a continual allowance given him of the king, a daily rate for every day, all the days of his life."

Matthew 6:11 — "Give us this day our daily bread."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's ordinary preservation of His promises looks like a daily ration, not a rescue.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The English word has narrowed to mean a regimen of eating, and nothing doctrinal is at stake in the drift. What is at stake is how the last paragraph of Jeremiah is read. A book that has spent fifty-two chapters on the destruction of Jerusalem ends with a released prisoner and a food allowance, and many readers pass over it as an administrative footnote. It is nothing of the sort. The covenant with David hung by this thread, and the thread is described as a continual diet… every day a portion… all the days of his life.

The principle to recover is patience with ordinary provision. God's way of keeping His promises is very often a daily ration at somebody else's table rather than a deliverance anyone would write a song about. Israel in the wilderness got manna each morning and no more; the widow of Zarephath got a barrel that did not empty rather than a granary; and the Lord taught His disciples to ask for bread this day. A church that can only see God at work in the spectacular will read Jeremiah 52 as an anticlimax, when it is in fact the hinge on which the genealogy of Christ turns.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew aruchah (H737), an allowance, a regular meal; debar yom beyomo, the portion of a day in its day; Greek diaita, manner of living.

expand to see more

Hebrew aruchah (H737) — an allowance, a settled ration; Jeremiah 52:34 and 2 Kings 25:30.

Hebrew aruchath tamid (H8548) — a continual allowance; tamid is the same word used of the continual burnt offering.

Hebrew debar yom beyomo — the matter of a day in its day; the manna formula of Exodus 16:4.

Greek epiousion (G1967) — daily, for the coming day; Matthew 6:11, the bread asked for one day at a time.

Greek diaita — a way of living; Webster's root, before the English narrowed it to regimen.

Usage

"“A continual diet… every day a portion… all the days of his life” — Jeremiah piles the words up."

"“He did continually eat bread before him” — the Davidic line, fed at a pagan table."

"“Give us this day our daily bread” — the same arrangement, taught as a prayer."
